entities.name: Nafi ibn al-Azraq
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Nafi ibn al-Azraq (d. 685 CE) was the eponymous founder and first leader of the Azariqa, the most radical and uncompromising sect within the Kharijite movement during the tumultuous Second Fitna (680-692 CE). Operating primarily from Basra and the southwestern Persian provinces of Khuzestan, his leadership defined an era of extreme militancy, where theological conviction translated into a policy of absolute rejection and violence against all who did not adhere to his group's strict interpretation of Islam, including other Kharijites and mainstream Muslims alike. His brief but impactful career established a precedent for religious extremism that reverberated through early Islamic history.

Following the death of Yazid I in 683 CE, and amidst the power vacuum and civil war of the Second Fitna, Nafi ibn al-Azraq seized control of Basra in 684 CE, expelling the Umayyad governor and establishing a short-lived Kharijite proto-state. His followers, who would become known as the Azariqa, then engaged in a campaign of terror and conquest across southern Iraq and Persia. They were notorious for their doctrine of *istihlal* (declaring the blood of opponents lawful) and *takfir* (excommunication), applying it even to women and children of those deemed apostates. This uncompromising stance alienated many, including other Kharijite factions, but drew fervent support from those seeking a puritanical interpretation of Islamic governance.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Nafi ibn al-Azraq was instrumental in defining the most extreme and violent strain of Kharijism, the Azariqa, whose campaigns devastated parts of Iraq and Persia for over two decades. His actions and doctrines left a lasting imprint on early Islamic political and theological thought, influencing perceptions of religious radicalism.
